dailyBrief.text: Tough morning, Cleveland: the Guardians' season ended last night in St. Petersburg, a 7-3 loss to Tampa Bay in ALCS Game 6 that sends the Rays to the World Series instead. Overnight, Zelenskiy arrived in Oslo for talks with U.S. envoy Witkoff and European leaders on ending the war, even as a Russian drone killed three people on the highway south of Kyiv. Closer to home, Nestlé confirmed it will close its Solon factory by the end of 2027 and move production to South Carolina — the campus stays, and the city is promising job help for affected workers. Solon woke up clear and cold at 37°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 68°. Today in town: the CLEO on the Go Luncheon at Mavis Public House at 11:30, and the Browns get a quiet week to enjoy first place before Sunday at Tennessee.

weekBrief.text: It's a crisp, dry fall week in Solon: sunny skies almost every day, highs in the mid-to-upper 60s and chilly nights in the 30s and 40s, with today topping out near 68°. The Guardians' October run is over after Monday's Game 6 loss, so the sports baton passes on: the Cavs open Thursday night at Philadelphia and play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, and the first-place Browns head to Tennessee on Sunday. Around town it's a full week — trunk-or-treat Thursday in Solon, Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls, and Barack Obama rallying in Cleveland on Saturday for the fall races, while Solon digests the news that Nestlé will wind down its factory here by the end of 2027. Grocery play of the week is still Giant Eagle's free-turkey deal — spend $350 by November 8 — and with the baby countdown very much on, it's a good week to knock a few more checklist items off together.

items.summary:
Voters in Alberta have decisively backed staying in Canada. With more than 1.5 million ballots counted in Monday's referendum, about 76 percent chose to remain part of the country, while roughly 24 percent supported starting a process that could eventually lead to separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.

The vote was not itself a decision to secede. A yes result would only have put the oil-rich province on a path toward a later, binding vote on independence. Premier Danielle Smith, who called the referendum under pressure from separatists inside her own United Conservative Party even though she opposes independence, welcomed the outcome, saying Albertans had chosen a stronger Alberta inside a united Canada.

The result is a clear win for Prime Minister Mark Carney, who campaigned for unity in the province last week and framed the vote as a test of national cohesion at a moment of trade conflict and annexation talk from the United States. Carney said the outcome lets the country move forward together on trade, infrastructure and energy, with Alberta at the center.

Separatist leaders noted that roughly a quarter of voters still backed their cause and argued the province's grievances with Ottawa over energy and federal policy have not gone away. Smith is expected to address the province Tuesday evening.
items.title: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject a move toward independence from Canada

items.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders, an effort to steady a relationship with Washington that has frayed badly over the past two weeks. Norway is hosting, Finland's president is taking part, and Jared Kushner was expected to join remotely.

Ahead of the meeting, Zelenskiy spoke by phone with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and said the conversation covered the issues Kyiv cares about most: ballistic missile interceptors to protect cities, reliable early warning of Russian missile launches, and restoring full use of the Starlink and Starshield satellite links Ukrainian forces rely on. Rubio's public line, echoed in reporting Tuesday, is that nothing is being deliberately withheld from Ukraine.

That assurance sits uneasily next to recent facts on the ground. Kyiv says it has missed early warnings three times in the past week, seen satellite links throttled, and waited on interceptor missiles its European partners already paid for, while President Trump has waived some Russia sanctions and said Moscow has behaved fine on Ukraine.

Watch for the joint press conference in Oslo later Tuesday, and for whether Witkoff's expected follow-on trip to brief President Putin produces a concrete proposal or just another round of statements.
items.title: In Oslo, Zelenskiy presses Witkoff as Rubio says nothing is being deliberately denied to Ukraine

items.summary:
Romania's parliament on Tuesday confirmed independent Luca Niculescu as prime minister, closing out almost six months without a fully empowered government. Niculescu, a 55-year-old former journalist who has served as a diplomat and deputy foreign minister, won the confidence vote with 280 votes, comfortably above the 233 he needed.

He was nominated by centrist President Nicusor Dan, whose fourth attempt to install a government this was. The previous broad pro-European coalition collapsed in early May, and the long stalemate since then has weighed on investor confidence and put pressure on the country's investment-grade credit rating. Niculescu will lead a minority government of leftists and technocrats.

His agenda is a hard one: shrink one of the European Union's largest budget deficits, support an economy that is contracting, scrap an extra turnover tax on companies, and find room to raise pensions that have been frozen for two years because of fiscal limits. Niculescu told lawmakers he was not asking for a blank check, only for a government with full powers after months of crisis.

Analysts warn the new government could be short-lived, given its minority status and the size of the economic repair job in a NATO and EU member state on the alliance's eastern flank.
items.title: Romania's parliament confirms a new prime minister and ends nearly six months of deadlock

items.summary:
Malaysia's Registrar of Societies on Tuesday cancelled the registration of Perikatan Nasional, the country's main opposition coalition, after a dispute between its two biggest parties. The move means the coalition's member parties cannot contest upcoming elections under a shared banner.

The fight is between PAS, the conservative Islamist party that holds more seats than any other single party in the 222-member parliament, and Bersatu, led by former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin. Bersatu had complained it was shut out of a coalition council meeting in July, calling it a breach of the coalition's constitution. The registrar said the explanation it received after a warning last month failed to answer the grounds for cancellation.

The timing matters. The state of Malacca votes on November 14, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's government has already lost two regional polls this year, and tensions inside his own ruling coalition have raised talk of an early general election. A divided opposition would normally be an opportunity for the government.

Perikatan Nasional's secretary-general condemned the decision as an attempt to weaken opponents before the Malacca vote and said the coalition will challenge the de-registration in court.
items.title: Malaysia cancels the registration of its main opposition coalition ahead of elections

items.summary:
The Bank of Israel is widely expected to leave its benchmark interest rate at 3.25 percent on Wednesday, pausing after three straight cuts in May, July and September. All 15 economists in a Reuters poll forecast a hold, even though inflation, at 1.6 percent in September, sits comfortably inside the government's 1 to 3 percent target range.

The decision lands six days before Israel's October 27 parliamentary election, the country's first vote since the October 7, 2023 attacks. Polls show neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor the main opposition grouping, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, clearly able to form a majority. Analysts say a cut this week could be read as helping the incumbent, and the central bank is unlikely to want that argument.

The economy itself is sending mixed signals. Growth rebounded sharply in the second quarter at a 15.4 percent annualized pace, but the shekel has slipped to a nine-month low against the dollar. Israel's easing cycle, five quarter-point cuts since last November, also runs against a global backdrop of generally tighter policy.

At least one more cut, to 3 percent, is widely expected after the election. Watch Wednesday's statement language for how explicitly the bank ties its next move to the vote being out of the way.
items.title: Israel's central bank is expected to pause rate cuts a week before the election

items.summary:
The European Commission said Tuesday it is looking at aligning two separate paperwork systems for employees who work temporarily in another EU country: the A1 social-security certificate and a new electronic declaration for posted workers that the European Parliament has just approved.

The A1 form proves a worker posted abroad stays covered by their home country's social-security system, and more than 5.6 million of them were issued across Europe in 2024. Employers have complained for years about the burden. The new eDeclaration law creates a single EU portal and a standard form for notifying authorities when staff are sent to another member state.

Lawmakers who steered the measure through described it as proof that simplification does not have to mean deregulation, and Europe's trade union confederation said the final text strengthened protections for workers and labor inspectors. Germany's engineering association welcomed it but cautioned it will only simplify life if enough member countries actually join the common portal.

It is inside-baseball Brussels, but it touches millions of workers and the companies that move them around the single market, and it signals where the EU's red-tape-cutting push goes next.
items.title: EU weighs merging worker-posting and social-security paperwork into one system

items.summary:
House Republicans are lowering expectations for the nationwide redistricting fight they expected to pad their majority, Axios reports. Strategists who once talked about a double-digit gain now privately worry the remapping war could net the party as little as one seat overall.

The math moved for several reasons. A Missouri map was thrown out by the courts, the national polling environment has darkened, with Democrats leading by about 8 points in new Washington Post-ABC polling, and Republican support among Latino voters has eroded in Texas and Florida, the two states where the party drew its most aggressive new maps. Party leaders have said publicly they would be surprised to sweep all five targeted Texas seats or all four in Florida.

On the other side, California Democrats engineered a map with four additional solidly Democratic seats and one more competitive seat, and Democrats sound confident they can win all five. In the worst case Republicans sketch for themselves, the two parties' gains nearly cancel out.

With the midterms two weeks away, redistricting looks less like the structural lock Republicans hoped for and more like an expensive draw, which puts even more weight on turnout and candidate quality in the newly drawn districts.
items.title: House Republicans quietly scale back hopes for a big redistricting boost

items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced trip to Israel on Monday, according to Axios reporting cited across outlets Tuesday. The meeting reportedly took place at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, where U.S. fighter jets and refueling aircraft are deployed, and Hegseth publicly highlighted a visit with American troops in the Central Command region.

The timing is doing a lot of work. The visit came eight days before Israel's parliamentary election and about two weeks before the U.S. midterms, and it landed amid Washington-Jerusalem discussions about possibly resuming large-scale operations against Iran. One senior military official quoted in Tuesday's coverage suggested American operations could intensify soon, though neither the Pentagon nor Israel's embassy in Washington commented on the substance of the talks.

Politically, the trip sits inside a split message from the administration. President Trump has given Netanyahu his complete and total endorsement for next week's election, while Vice President JD Vance has pointedly declined to endorse, saying his focus is the American midterms.

Watch for any visible force movements around Ovda and other regional bases, and for whether talk of a post-election offensive hardens into announced operations once both countries' votes are done.
items.title: Hegseth's quiet Netanyahu meeting fuels talk of a renewed U.S. push against Iran

items.summary:
The United States ran a budget deficit of about $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended September 30, the largest since 2021 and the third-largest ever recorded. Axios highlighted the new figures Tuesday, and the underlying Treasury and Congressional Budget Office numbers show revenue rising about 3 percent while spending rose about 6 percent, to roughly $7.4 trillion.

The biggest driver is the cost of carrying the debt itself. Net interest payments set records, topping $1.1 trillion on the CBO's accounting and consuming more than a fifth of federal tax receipts, as higher interest rates, partly reflecting inflation pressure from the Iran war, met a national debt that has passed $40 trillion in total. Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and defense spending all rose as well.

A $2 trillion gap in a growing economy with low unemployment is what worries budget analysts most. It equals about 6.2 percent of the economy, roughly double the share economists typically call sustainable, and debt held by the public now rivals the size of the entire economy, a level last seen around World War II.

Nobody serious expects a default, but the arithmetic narrows future choices: every additional point of interest expense is money that cannot go to programs, tax cuts or emergencies, and the midterm campaigns are now arguing over that constraint in real time.
items.title: The federal deficit hit $2 trillion, the largest since the pandemic climb-out

items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear an appeal from Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two co-defendants who wanted to restore plea agreements that would have spared them the death penalty for the September 11 attacks. The unsigned order drew no noted dissents, and Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate.

The deals, reached in July 2024, would have traded guilty pleas for life sentences without parole for Mohammed, Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi. Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin revoked them two days later, arguing only the defense secretary should decide whether death stays on the table for an attack that killed 2,977 people. A divided federal appeals court upheld Austin's authority to withdraw the agreements.

The case now returns to the military commission at Guantanamo Bay, where a trial is set for June 2028, more than 25 years after the attacks. Prosecutors face a serious hole: a military judge ruled in August that Mohammed's confession to FBI agents was not voluntary and cannot be used, removing what the government had called the centerpiece of its case.

Families of victims remain split, some seeing a full trial as the only route to real justice and others viewing the plea deals as the best hope of ever closing a case that has been in pretrial litigation for well over a decade.
items.title: Supreme Court won't revive the 9/11 plea deal, leaving a 2028 death-penalty trial as the path

items.summary:
President Trump used a social media post to give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu his complete and total endorsement in next week's Israeli election, praising him as a partner in confronting Iran and warning that any other leader would leave work America is not inclined to do itself. The endorsement had been withheld for months as the two leaders' strategies diverged.

Vice President JD Vance took the opposite approach in an interview Monday. He said he endorses American candidates, that his focus is the midterms, and that he is neither endorsing nor anti-endorsing Netanyahu, a notable contrast given that Vance traveled to Budapest earlier this year to back Viktor Orban in Hungary's election.

Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, though polling also suggests the opposition may struggle to assemble a government of its own. Trump remains popular in Israel, but commentators there have expressed disappointment with the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and a ceasefire proposal many felt fell short of the war's stated aims.

The split at the top of the U.S. ticket is itself a signal: Washington's two most likely future standard-bearers are already advertising different instincts about how personally to intervene in an ally's politics.
items.title: Trump backs Netanyahu completely; Vance pointedly stays out of Israel's election

items.summary:
Technology shares led a Monday rebound on Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.11 percent to 26,430.89, the S&P 500 added 0.41 percent to 7,690.73, and the Dow slipped slightly. Chipmakers did the heavy lifting: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained 1.61 percent, ending an eight-session losing streak, its longest since 2008.

The bond market moved the other way. The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.15 percent, up from 5.09 percent, with the 2-year at 4.77 percent and the 30-year at 5.48 percent. Underneath the index gains, breadth was weak, with decliners outnumbering advancers on the New York Stock Exchange and the equal-weight S&P 500 fund actually falling.

The Federal Reserve is now in its blackout period ahead of the October 27-28 meeting. Chair Kevin Warsh's remarks in Bangkok last week were the last public words from any Fed official before the decision, and futures pricing put roughly a 72 percent chance on rates staying unchanged this month, with most traders expecting a quarter-point hike in December instead.

That combination, expensive AI stocks and a 5 percent-plus 10-year yield, is the tension hanging over the roughly 70 S&P 500 earnings reports due this week.
items.title: Chip stocks snap an eight-day slide and lift the Nasdaq, even as Treasury yields climb

items.summary:
General Motors reported a strong third quarter on Tuesday. Net income reached $3.3 billion, up 151 percent from a year earlier, revenue grew about 3 percent to $50.0 billion, and adjusted earnings of $3.70 per share beat Wall Street's estimates. North America was the engine, with adjusted operating profit there up more than 43 percent as margins widened.

GM credited spending discipline, firm pricing and record sales of its full-size pickup trucks, along with its best fleet sales pace since 2019. The year-ago quarter was weighed down by electric vehicle restructuring, and GM says it has now recorded $11.2 billion of EV-related charges since it began reshaping that business in late 2025. The company also authorized a new $20 billion multi-year share repurchase and declared an 18-cent quarterly dividend.

Investors focused on the outlook instead. GM tightened its full-year guidance ranges, flagged roughly $2 billion of commodity inflation plus logistics and raw-material cost pressure, and its shares fell sharply in pre-market trading despite the beat.

The split reaction captures the auto industry's moment: today's truck profits are real, but investors are pricing tomorrow's costs, tariffs and the expensive EV transition more than the quarter just printed.
items.title: GM's profit more than doubles and it adds a $20 billion buyback, but the stock still falls

items.summary:
Asian technology shares had another rough Tuesday. SK Hynix fell more than 4 percent to its lowest level since April, extending a slide that has erased about 31 percent of its value in October, and its weight dragged South Korea's Kospi down sharply. Japan's Nikkei and Hong Kong's Hang Seng also fell.

A second data point rattled the same trade. Elice, a South Korean data-center provider, plunged roughly a third on its first day of trading in Seoul, a weak debut that revived questions about how much investors will pay for AI infrastructure. SoftBank's credit risk, measured by default swaps, has climbed to its highest in nearly four years amid concern over the funding behind its AI bets.

The worries are familiar by now: heavy borrowing to build data centers, rising Chinese competition, tight memory supply, and the possibility of higher interest rates. Chip stocks have swung between relief rallies and sell-offs for weeks, and Monday's U.S. rebound did not travel across the Pacific.

Nvidia chief Jensen Huang has told investors the turbulence will pass and to focus on long-term value. This week's U.S. tech earnings will test whether Wall Street agrees with him or with Seoul.
items.title: In Asia, the AI trade wobbles again: SK Hynix slides and a data-center debut flops

items.summary:
Tuesday is one of the heaviest days of earnings season. General Motors, GE Aerospace and 3M reported in the morning, with GE posting a 25 percent jump in revenue and raising its outlook, while futures pointed lower as oil traded at its highest levels in months and investors braced for the afternoon reports.

The after-close lineup is the headline act. Netflix reports, United Airlines reports, and SpaceX delivers only its second earnings release ever, an event that draws attention well beyond space investors because of how much government and commercial launch business now runs through the company. Hasbro and Halliburton also beat expectations earlier in the day, Hasbro on digital gaming strength.

One policy item shares the business agenda: the federal government has banned the Chinese AI model DeepSeek from government agency systems, a decision with direct consequences for vendors selling AI tools into Washington.

With the Nasdaq coming off a 1 percent-plus rebound day and crude above $100, tonight's results will help decide whether Monday's recovery was a trend or a pause.
items.title: A stacked earnings day: GM and GE this morning, Netflix, SpaceX and United after the close

items.summary:
Cleveland-based steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs reported a return to profit in the third quarter and set an ambitious target of more than $4 billion in earnings for 2027. The results, released Monday, sent the shares up more than 7 percent as analysts flagged a buy signal on the stock.

The improvement reflects stronger steel volumes and pricing, with anticipated tariff protection for domestic producers cited as a key support. For a company that has spent years digesting big acquisitions in steel and iron ore, a clean profitable quarter paired with a specific, large 2027 target gives investors something concrete to model.

Cliffs matters beyond its ticker in Northeast Ohio. It is one of the region's signature industrial employers and a bellwether for the auto and manufacturing supply chains that run through the Great Lakes.

The open question is durability: whether tariff support and volume growth hold through 2027, and whether the company converts the earnings outlook into sustained cash generation rather than a single strong year.
items.title: Cleveland-Cliffs swings back to profit and targets more than $4 billion in 2027 earnings

items.summary:
AI company Anthropic and infrastructure provider Nscale are reportedly in talks on another computing deal valued around $45 billion, according to TechCrunch reporting. If completed, it would be the pair's second arrangement at that scale, and one of the largest single compute commitments in the industry.

Deals like this are how the AI buildout actually gets financed: model companies lock in years of data-center capacity, and infrastructure firms use those commitments to raise the debt and equity to build. The scale explains both the excitement and the growing anxiety in credit markets, where default-insurance costs on big AI borrowers have been climbing.

The reported talks also underline how concentrated the boom has become. A small number of model labs account for a large share of global data-center demand, which means a slowdown at any one of them would ripple quickly through chipmakers, utilities and lenders.

Nothing has been announced by either company, so treat the figure as reported rather than confirmed. Confirmation, and the financing structure behind it, would be the real story.
items.title: Anthropic and Nscale are reportedly talking about a second $45 billion compute deal

items.source: USA Today Network / Democrat and Chronicle
items.summary:
A North Carolina compounding pharmacy, Apothecary Pharma, is recalling 22 vials of its compounded tirzepatide injection, the active ingredient in brand-name drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, over possible contamination. The recall, classified as Class II, also covers a NAD+ injection the company makes. Class II means use could cause temporary or medically reversible health effects, with serious consequences considered unlikely.

The affected tirzepatide is an 18 mg/mL solution in 4 mL multi-dose vials, sold by prescription, across 22 listed lot numbers with beyond-use dates running from October 7 through late November 2026. The brand-name drugs themselves are not part of the recall. Because Apothecary supplies several telehealth providers, patients may hold an affected vial even if they never dealt with the pharmacy directly, so the label and lot number are what to check.

The company was already on the FDA's radar. It received a warning letter in December 2025 citing serious deficiencies in its practices for making sterile drugs, which the agency said put patients at risk. Compounded GLP-1 drugs have drawn extra scrutiny since the official shortages of tirzepatide and semaglutide ended in late 2024 and early 2025.

Anyone with an affected lot should not use it and should contact their prescriber for instructions. Neither the FDA nor the company had issued detailed public disposal guidance as of Tuesday's reporting.
items.title: Compounded GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide over possible contamination

items.summary:
The Justice Department has charged 28 people in California with voting crimes, NPR reported in its Tuesday morning brief. The charges are the latest visible step in a broader federal focus on election integrity heading into the final two weeks before the midterms.

Details of the individual cases, including how many involve noncitizen voting allegations versus other offenses, are still emerging. Federal voting prosecutions are typically built case by case, and charges are allegations until tested in court. The announcement's timing, two weeks before Election Day, guarantees it will be read politically as well as legally, by both parties.

The California cases land in a national argument that is already running hot: the administration wants expanded federal access to state voter data and citizenship records, while many state officials, including in Ohio's secretary of state race, are campaigning on exactly the opposite philosophy of state control.

Watch for the charging documents themselves. The specific statutes used and the evidence described will say more about the scale of this effort than the headline number does.
items.title: Justice Department charges 28 people in California with voting-related crimes

items.summary:
The federal government has directed agencies to remove the Chinese AI model DeepSeek from most civilian government systems, according to the official notice reported Tuesday. The order cites the risk of sensitive data being transferred to China through the model's services.

DeepSeek startled the industry in 2025 by releasing capable models built, it said, at a fraction of U.S. training costs, and its tools spread quickly through consumer apps and developer platforms. U.S. officials have since treated its data practices as a security question, not just a competition story, and several states and federal bodies had already restricted it on government devices.

A government-wide removal order raises the stakes for contractors and software vendors, who now have to certify that DeepSeek components are not embedded anywhere in tools they sell to agencies. That kind of supply-chain check is slower and harder than simply uninstalling an app.

Watch for the compliance deadlines in the fine print, and for whether defense and intelligence systems, which run under separate rules, adopt parallel bans.
items.title: U.S. orders the DeepSeek AI model removed from most civilian government systems

items.summary:
President Trump said the United States and Mexico are close to what he called a great trade agreement, Reuters reported. No text or detailed terms have been released, so what close means in practice, on tariffs, autos, agriculture or migration-linked provisions, is not yet public.

Mexico is the United States' largest goods trading partner, and any revision ripples straight into Midwest manufacturing. Auto parts, steel and finished vehicles cross the border multiple times during production, which is why Ohio suppliers watch U.S.-Mexico talks as closely as they watch Detroit's earnings.

Both governments have incentives to announce progress before the U.S. midterms, and both have used that calendar before. Markets took the comment in stride on Tuesday, treating it as a signal to watch rather than a finished deal.

The test will be specifics: tariff rates, rules of origin and enforcement language, published in a form Congress and industry can actually read.
items.title: Trump says the U.S. and Mexico are close to a 'great' trade deal

items.summary:
San Francisco wide receiver Mike Evans left Monday night's game against Washington late in the first half after going down without contact on a 16-yard catch from Brock Purdy. He grabbed at his lower leg and Achilles, limped to the locker room, and was ruled out for the rest of the game with an Achilles injury.

Evans was San Francisco's leading receiver this season and had already produced before the injury, catching three passes for 94 yards including a 54-yard play early in the game. He had been questionable all week after missing practice with rib and Achilles issues, which will sharpen questions about whether he should have played.

A confirmed Achilles tear would likely end his season and change the 49ers' offense, which leans on his downfield presence. Non-contact lower-leg injuries to veteran receivers tend to draw cautious prognoses until imaging is done.

Expect an MRI update from the team in the next day or two. Until then, San Francisco's passing game planning for next week carries a large asterisk.
items.title: 49ers receiver Mike Evans leaves Monday Night Football with an Achilles injury

items.summary:
Minutes after Tampa Bay eliminated the Guardians with a 7-3 win in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night, veteran catcher Austin Hedges sat in the visiting clubhouse at Tropicana Field and got emotional about his future. Hedges is a free agent this offseason, so the loss may have been his final game in a Cleveland uniform. He said plainly that he hopes it is not, and that he loves it in Cleveland.

His history with the club runs in two acts. Cleveland first acquired him from San Diego in 2020, he left for Pittsburgh and Texas in 2023 and won a World Series ring with the Rangers, then chose to come back in 2024. Since then he has re-signed on one-year deals each winter, saying he wants to finish his career here.

Hedges' value has never been his bat. It is game-calling, defense, and a clubhouse presence younger pitchers lean on, which is exactly the profile teams keep on short contracts into a player's mid-30s, and exactly the kind a front office can also talk itself out of in November.

Cleveland's catching picture behind him will shape the decision quickly. Expect his name to be one of the first small dominoes of the Guardians' offseason.
items.title: 'I hope this isn't the last time I put a Cleveland jersey on': Hedges faces free agency

items.summary:
One of the strangest facts of the Guardians' ALCS loss is that Tanner Bibee, the club's Opening Day starter and its leader in starts and innings this season, did not throw a single pitch in the six-game series. In Monday's elimination game Cleveland used eight pitchers in a bullpen game while Bibee watched.

Manager Stephen Vogt addressed it directly after the game. The plan, he said, was to hold Bibee as the long-relief option for a game that ran deep into extra innings and needed multiple frames covered. None of the six games went past nine innings, so the spot never arrived. Vogt added that had Cleveland advanced, Bibee's role in the World Series would have looked very different, and called the outcome unfortunate.

The explanation is coherent, but it will be debated all winter. Through six innings Monday the bullpen had allowed only three earned runs; the game broke on two-run homers by Junior Caminero off Cade Smith and Yandy Diaz off Hunter Gaddis. Critics will argue an elimination game is precisely when you use your best rested arm before the game is gone, not after.

Either way, the Guardians head into the offseason with a rested ace, a list of bullpen questions, and a manager whose biggest October decision was one he never got to make.
items.title: Vogt explains the ALCS mystery: Tanner Bibee was being saved for extra innings that never came

items.summary:
The 4-2 Browns, alone in first place in the AFC North after Sunday's 13-10 win over Baltimore, travel to face the 1-5 Titans on Sunday as favorites for the first time this season, opening as roughly 2-point favorites with a low total of 36.5. Tennessee just won its first game, rallying past Indianapolis, which is part of the problem, local analysts argued Tuesday.

The warning making the rounds is that this game carries more pressure than the Ravens game did. A division win at home raised expectations; a loss as favorites to a one-win team would hand momentum back and tighten the division race. Cleveland already lived the ugly version of this script in Week 5, losing 17-12 to the Jets in the rain at MetLife.

Meanwhile, the November 10 trade deadline suddenly matters in the buyers' direction. Cleveland.com's Orange and Brown Talk crew spent Tuesday asking what a 4-2 team should shop for, and how much it should be willing to pay, with Deshaun Watson's uneven play and the offense's struggles framing every answer.

Kickoff in Nashville is Sunday at 1 p.m. ET on CBS. A win sends Cleveland to Pittsburgh at 5-2 with genuine control of the division race; a loss makes the deadline conversation much more complicated.
items.title: First-place Browns are favorites at Tennessee, and that's exactly the trap, analysts warn

items.summary:
The Cavaliers announced Tuesday that forward Nae'Qwan Tomlin has a lower back stress reaction and will be reevaluated in about three to four weeks. Tomlin missed the entire preseason with the problem and had still not been cleared to practice, so the update confirms his season debut will be significantly delayed.

On the short end of the timeline he would miss at least the first 11 games of Cleveland's season, starting with Thursday's opener at Philadelphia and Saturday's home opener against Brooklyn, and a realistic return likely runs longer. Tomlin, who turns 26 in December, earned his spot last season, averaging 5.8 points and 2.9 rebounds in 15.7 minutes across 64 games and converting his two-way deal into a guaranteed two-year contract in February.

The absence tightens an already thin roster. Cleveland is carrying only 14 standard contracts, and another frontcourt player, Khalifa Diop, is dealing with a knee injury and was not expected to play a real role. Sam Merrill, Mario Hezonja and Jaylon Tyson project as the main bench wings and forwards in Kenny Atkinson's rotation.

Stress reactions are managed with rest rather than procedures, so the reevaluation in late November is the next real checkpoint. The Cavs' early-season depth will be tested before it.
items.title: Cavs forward Nae'Qwan Tomlin will miss at least 3-4 weeks with a back injury

items.summary:
Cleveland City Council moved from discussion to decision on Monday, passing a set of emergency ordinances that included extending the moratorium on data-center permit reviews into early 2027. The extension ordinance passed 11-1 with rules suspended for final passage, alongside a resolution opposing proposed federal Census rule changes that drew unanimous sponsorship.

The moratorium, first imposed for three months in mid-July, was set to expire this week. Three town halls this fall drew residents worried about the regional power grid, Lake Erie water use, noise and whether hyperscale facilities create enough local jobs to justify tax incentives. Council members said the extra months are for writing permanent rules on zoning, power and water rather than rushing a decision.

The fight is really about Cleveland Public Power and the wider PJM grid. Council legislation already bars data companies from misusing CPP, which serves about 74,000 customers, but a grid emergency two states away can still hit Northeast Ohio, a point council members made repeatedly during the hearings. Ohio already hosts about 283 data centers statewide.

More legislation scrutinizing data-center growth is expected by the end of January, which is when the temporary pause stops being a pause and becomes a policy.
items.title: Cleveland City Council votes to extend the data center moratorium into early 2027

items.summary:
Signal Ohio's voter guide, published Tuesday, lays out how sharply Republican Robert Sprague and Democrat Allison Russo differ on the mechanics of voting: voter ID law, drop boxes, redistricting and how seriously to treat election fraud claims. Libertarian Tom Pruss is also on the November 3 ballot. The winner succeeds term-limited Frank LaRose, who is running for state auditor.

The secretary of state is Ohio's chief elections officer, training county officials, investigating fraud allegations and reviewing petitions, with seats on both the Ohio Redistricting Commission and the Ballot Board, which approves the wording voters read on statewide issues. The office also registers new businesses and trademarks, the quieter half of the job.

The race mirrors the national fight in miniature. Sprague's campaign emphasizes working with the Trump administration on access to federal citizenship data and added ballot security measures. Russo, a state representative and former House minority leader from Upper Arlington, campaigns on bipartisan election administration and protecting access.

With every Ohio executive office turning over this cycle, this is the down-ballot race with the most direct effect on how the 2028 presidential election gets run in a perennial battleground. Early voting patterns this fall, shifting from mail toward in-person, will be its first live test.
items.title: Ohio's secretary of state race is really an argument about how elections should run
